title: Plant and Animal Transport Systems
description: Phloem and xylem in plants, transpiration, blood vessels and the heart, plus the lung and digestive systems.
hero_image_caption: A scanning electron micrograph reveals the hollow tubes of xylem vessels carrying water and minerals through a plant stem — the plant world's equivalent of an arterial highway.
content_html:
Why Do Large Organisms Need Transport Systems?

Single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion alone to supply all their needs — their high surface area to volume (SA:V) ratio means diffusion distances are short. But as organisms get larger, their SA:V ratio decreases, and diffusion becomes too slow to supply oxygen and nutrients to cells deep inside the body, or to remove waste products efficiently. Multicellular organisms therefore evolved dedicated transport systems alongside specialised exchange surfaces.

Plant Transport — Xylem and Phloem

Plants have two types of transport tissue bundled together in vascular bundles: xylem and phloem.

Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots to leaves. The cells are dead and form hollow tubes with thick walls reinforced with lignin, which makes them rigid and waterproof and provides structural support for the plant. Water moves through xylem as an unbroken column pulled upwards by evaporation from the leaves — this is the transpiration stream.

Phloem tubes transport dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) from the leaves — where they are made by photosynthesis — to the rest of the plant, including roots, growing tips and storage organs. This process is called translocation. Unlike xylem, phloem cells are living and have sieve plates (pores) to allow the flow of sucrose. Translocation requires energy and can move substances both up and down the plant.

Key Fact

Xylem: dead hollow tubes reinforced with lignin; transports water and minerals upwards. Phloem: living tubes with sieve plates; transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) up and down by translocation. Both found in vascular bundles.

Transpiration

Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour from the leaves through tiny pores called stomata. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, more water is drawn up through the xylem from the roots — creating the transpiration stream. Guard cells open and close the stomata: they become turgid (absorb water, swell, open stoma) in light, and flaccid (lose water, close stoma) in darkness or drought conditions.

Four environmental factors increase the rate of transpiration:

Light intensity — causes stomata to open wider, increasing water loss. Temperature — increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, speeding up evaporation. Wind/air movement — removes humid air from around the leaf, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for water vapour to diffuse out. Humidity — low humidity (dry air) increases the concentration gradient, speeding up water loss; high humidity slows it.

A potometer is used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant cutting, which is taken as a proxy for the rate of transpiration. The distance moved by an air bubble in a capillary tube per unit time is recorded as conditions are varied.

The Human Circulatory System

Humans have a double circulatory system: one circuit pumps blood from the heart to the lungs for gas exchange (pulmonary circuit), and the other pumps oxygenated blood from the heart to the body (systemic circuit). This maintains high blood pressure for efficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients.

The heart has four chambers — two atria (receive blood) and two ventricles (pump blood out). The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it needs to generate higher pressure to pump blood around the whole body. Valves prevent backflow and ensure blood flows in one direction.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular walls with elastic fibres to withstand the surge of blood with each heartbeat. Their lumen (internal channel) is relatively small.

Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls and a larger lumen. They contain valves to prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart.

Capillaries are microscopic vessels with walls just one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances by diffusion between the blood and surrounding tissues. Oxygen and glucose diffuse out; carbon dioxide and waste diffuse in.

Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape increases surface area for oxygen absorption. White blood cells are part of the immune system — phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies. Platelets are cell fragments that help blood to clot at wound sites. Plasma is the liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, carbon dioxide and antibodies.

Key Fact

Blood flow through the double circulatory system: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The left ventricle has thicker walls than the right because it pumps blood further.

Gas Exchange — The Lungs

The lungs are the site of gas exchange between the blood and the air. They contain millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange with features that are the same as other exchange surfaces: very large total surface area, walls just one cell thick to minimise diffusion distance, moist inner surface to allow gases to dissolve, and a rich network of capillaries to maintain steep concentration gradients by removing oxygen and delivering carbon dioxide.

The Digestive System

The digestive system breaks down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Key organs include the stomach (acid environment, protease enzymes break down proteins), the small intestine (enzymes from the pancreas complete digestion; products absorbed through villi into the blood), and the large intestine (water reabsorbed). The liver produces bile, which emulsifies fats (breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing the surface area for lipase enzymes to act on).

The inner wall of the small intestine is lined with millions of finger-like projections called villi, each covered in even smaller microvilli (the brush border). Together these massively increase the surface area for absorption. Each villus contains a dense capillary network (for absorbing glucose and amino acids into the blood) and a lacteal (a lymph vessel for absorbing fatty acids and glycerol from digested fats).

Villi share the same adaptations as other exchange surfaces: large surface area, thin walls (one cell thick), and a good blood supply to maintain steep concentration gradients. Glucose and amino acids are absorbed by a combination of diffusion and active transport; water is absorbed by osmosis.
exam_tip_html: For xylem vs phloem questions, remember the key distinctions: xylem is dead, lignin-reinforced, unidirectional (upward), transports water and minerals; phloem is living, bidirectional, transports sucrose by translocation. For blood vessel questions, structure always links to function: arteries have thick elastic walls for high pressure; veins have valves for low-pressure return; capillaries are one cell thick for diffusion. Never confuse atria and ventricles — atria receive, ventricles pump.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Xylem (dead, lignin-reinforced) transports water and minerals upwards by the transpiration stream. Phloem (living) transports sucrose by translocation, both up and down. Stomata control water loss — guard cells regulate their opening.
  • The human double circulatory system: heart (4 chambers, left ventricle thickest), arteries (high pressure, away from heart), veins (low pressure, valves, to heart), capillaries (1 cell thick, exchange surface).
  • Alveoli (lungs) and villi (small intestine) share common exchange surface adaptations: large surface area, thin walls, good blood supply. Both maximise the rate of substance movement by diffusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes phloem tissue?
A) Dead cells reinforced with lignin that transport water upwards
B) Living cells with sieve plates that transport sucrose up and down
C) Dead cells that transport mineral ions by active transport
D) Living cells that carry oxygen-rich blood to tissues
practice_questions.marks: B) Living cells with sieve plates that transport sucrose up and down [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two features of alveoli that make them efficient gas exchange surfaces.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (1 mark for any two correct):
• Large total surface area
• Thin walls (one cell thick) to minimise diffusion distance
• Moist inner surface to allow gases to dissolve
• Rich capillary network to maintain steep concentration gradients
[1 mark for two correct features]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between arteries and veins.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back to the heart (1)
• Arteries have thicker, more muscular and elastic walls than veins (1)
• Arteries carry blood at high pressure; veins carry blood at low pressure (1)
• Veins contain valves to prevent backflow; arteries do not (1)
• Arteries have a smaller lumen; veins have a larger lumen (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how xylem vessels are adapted for transporting water from the roots to the leaves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Xylem cells are dead and hollow, forming continuous tubes for water to flow through with little resistance (1)
• The walls are reinforced with lignin, which is waterproof and rigid — preventing the vessels from collapsing under the tension created by the transpiration stream (1)
• Water is drawn upwards continuously as it evaporates from the leaves through stomata (the transpiration stream), creating a 'pull' / cohesion-tension that maintains the water column (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: In bright sunlight, the transpiration rate of a plant is measured as 3.6 cm³ of water lost per hour. When a fan is added to increase air movement, the rate increases to 5.4 cm³ per hour. Calculate the percentage increase in transpiration rate. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage increase = (change ÷ original) × 100 (1)
Change = 5.4 − 3.6 = 1.8 cm³/hour (1)
Percentage increase = (1.8 ÷ 3.6) × 100 (1)
= 50% (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare how substances are transported in plants and in humans. Include reference to the structures involved and the mechanisms used.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• In plants, xylem transports water and minerals upwards from roots to leaves by the transpiration stream — passive process driven by evaporation (1)
• Phloem transports sucrose (from photosynthesis) up and down the plant by translocation — requires energy (active process) (1)
• In humans, the double circulatory system uses the heart to pump blood — right side to lungs, left side to body (1)
• Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; veins return blood at low pressure using valves to prevent backflow; capillaries allow exchange with tissues (1)
• Blood plasma transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and CO₂; red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin (1)
• Both plant and human systems use exchange surfaces with large surface area, thin walls and good supply of the transport medium to maximise diffusion rates (alveoli/villi in humans; root hair cells/stomata in plants) (1)

StudyVault Mastering: plant and human transport both covered in detail, with mechanisms (passive/active) distinguished and structural adaptations linked to function.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of blood vessel contains valves to prevent backflow?
What substance is transported by phloem?
Which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall: _____
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Left ventricle.

knowledge_checks.q: A plant is placed in windy conditions. What happens to the rate of transpiration and why: _____
options: Decreases, because wind cools the leaf
Increases, because wind removes humid air from around stomata, maintaining a steep concentration gradient
Stays the same, because transpiration depends only on light
Increases, because wind forces water up the xylem faster
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Increases, because wind removes humid air from around stomata, maintaining a steep concentration gradient.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between xylem and phloem?
flashcard_questions.a: Xylem: dead, lignin-reinforced, transports water and minerals upwards only (transpiration stream). Phloem: living, transports dissolved sucrose up and down by translocation, requires energy.
The loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata, which creates a 'pull' drawing water up through the xylem from the roots — the transpiration stream.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four factors that increase the rate of transpiration.
flashcard_questions.a: Higher light intensity (stomata open wider), higher temperature (faster evaporation), increased air movement/wind (removes humid air), lower humidity (steeper concentration gradient).

flashcard_questions.q: Describe the double circulatory system in humans.
flashcard_questions.a: Two circuits: pulmonary circuit (heart → lungs for gas exchange → heart) and systemic circuit (heart → body → heart).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right ventricle?
flashcard_questions.a: The left ventricle pumps blood around the entire body (systemic circuit), requiring higher pressure than the right ventricle, which only pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: What are villi and how are they adapted for absorption?
flashcard_questions.a: Finger-like projections lining the small intestine. Adaptations: large surface area (including microvilli), thin walls (one cell thick), dense capillary network, and lacteals for fat absorption.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the function of haemoglobin in red blood cells?
flashcard_questions.a: Haemoglobin is a red protein that binds to oxygen in the lungs (forming oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it to tissues where oxygen concentration is lower.

glossary_terms.definition: Dead, hollow tubes reinforced with lignin that transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots to leaves by the transpiration stream.
Living tubes with sieve plates that transport dissolved sugars (sucrose) from leaves to the rest of the plant by translocation.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant through the stomata, which creates a 'pull' drawing water up through the xylem from the roots.
Tiny pores on the underside of leaves that open and close to control gas exchange and water loss. Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells.
A circulatory system where blood flows through the heart twice for each complete circuit: once to the lungs (pulmonary circuit) and once to the body (systemic circuit).
Tiny air sacs in the lungs with a large total surface area, thin walls and a rich blood supply — adaptations for efficient gas exchange.
A red protein in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. It gives blood its red colour.
Bundles of xylem and phloem tissue found throughout the stem, roots and leaves of a plant, responsible for transporting water, minerals and dissolved sugars.
A tough, waterproof polymer that reinforces xylem cell walls, making them rigid and waterproof and providing structural support for the plant.
